Teladoc Health is expanding its Comprehensive Weight Care program with a newly introduced option that allows employers to contribute to GLP-1 costs outside of traditional pharmacy benefit designs.

Through the newly introduced offering, employers can give access to medications from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk—accompanied by support from licensed professionals, personalized lifestyle coaching, artificial intelligence-enabled food logging and more.

With each plan year, employers will set a fixed payment per employee per fill that applies consistently across covered medications, the company said. Employees then pay the remaining balance for each fill. Teladoc manages eligibility, program oversight and consolidated invoicing.

Pharmacy claims are administered on a 100% pass-through basis, including eligibility verification and audit-ready claims documentation.

Moreover, employers can opt in to tie contributions to program engagement, using metrics like food logging and regular weigh-ins, executives say.

Sources indicate that the offering is available now, with initial contracted clients slated to launch programs for their employees beginning Jan. 1, 2027.

“Employers want to provide benefits that help their workforce achieve their health goals and need flexible strategies that work for their organizations,” remarked Kelly Bliss, Teladoc Health U.S. Group Health president, in a statement. “We are helping employers meet the needs of their employees while providing greater predictability and transparency around healthcare spending. Importantly, we give people a trusted path to high-quality care and affordable access to FDA-approved, authentic medication for meaningful, sustained health outcomes.”.

Alongside the announcement, the firm also unveiled new research examining two years of weight-loss outcomes among nearly 23,000 members enrolled in its programs.

According to recent reports, results indicated “clinically meaningful weight loss” increased over time, with 47.7% of members achieving at least 5% weight loss by 24 months. And among those who lost weight during their first year, 53% continued losing additional weight during the second.

Tech Report: Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels.
  • The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways.
  • Recent findings suggest that testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels. Researchers found that men who ate more animal protein tended to have lower testosterone concentrations in their blood, while those who consumed more plant protein generally had higher levels.

The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways. However, the researchers caution that the differences were relatively small and that the results do not establish whether protein intake directly influences testosterone.

Recent findings suggest that testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function. Although age, excess body weight, and lifestyle habits are known to influence testosterone levels, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how diet, especially protein consumption, might be associated with this hormone.

Study of More Than 2,500 Men Reveals Contrasting Protein Patterns.

To investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed information from 2,546 men between the ages of 42 and 60 who lived in eastern Finland. The participants were part of the ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, a research project conducted at the University of Eastern Finland.

In a recent development, between 1984 and 1989, the men recorded everything they ate over four days, allowing researchers to evaluate their dietary habits and protein sources. Blood samples were also collected to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), a protein that helps regulate the amount of testosterone circulating in the bloodstream.

Industry observers note that the researchers then divided the participants into four groups based on their protein consumption. A clear contrast emerged when they compared the men with the highest and lowest intakes of animal and plant protein.

Industry observers note that men who consumed the most animal protein had average total testosterone concentrations 1.2 nmol/l lower than those who consumed the least. Plant protein indicated the opposite pattern, with men in the highest intake group having testosterone concentrations 1.1 nmol/l higher than those in the lowest group.

Similar relationships were observed for SHBG concentrations. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index, and several other factors related to diet, lifestyle, and health.

Dairy and Plant Proteins Show Different Testosterone Links.

A closer examination of individual protein sources revealed additional differences. Higher consumption of protein from dairy products was associated with lower concentrations of both total testosterone and SHBG.

Meanwhile, men who obtained more plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products tended to have higher total testosterone concentrations.

In a recent development, meat protein highlighted a somewhat different relationship. Although greater meat protein intake was linked to lower SHBG concentrations, researchers did not find a corresponding association with total testosterone levels.

These distinctions suggest that the relationship between dietary protein and male hormones may vary depending on where the protein comes from, rather than simply how much protein a person consumes.

What the Findings Mean for Men's Health.

According to recent reports, despite the contrasting patterns, the researchers emphasize that the observed testosterone differences were modest. It is also unknown whether changes of this size have any meaningful consequences for health.

"Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health," states Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

Recent findings suggest that an important limitation is that the research was cross-sectional, meaning dietary intake and hormone measurements were examined without tracking how changes in protein consumption affected testosterone over time. As a result, the findings cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

It has been revealed that other dietary characteristics or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. The researchers also cannot determine whether eating different types of protein influences testosterone production or changes how the hormone functions in the body.

For now, the findings highlight an interesting connection between protein sources and testosterone levels, while leaving open the question of whether changing protein choices could have any direct effect on male hormone health.

Materials provided by University of Eastern Finland. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#133624. 8 Things Your iPhone Does As You Flip Your Car Down An Embankment

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2086 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

8 Things Your iPhone Does As You Flip Your Car Down An Embankment

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A phone puts in a lot of work while we're driving around, especially if your car's infotainment system is painfully old and it's doing double duty there.
  • Apple introduced Crash Detection with the iPhone 14 in 2022 (it works on iPhone 14 or later running iOS 16 or later).
  • Industry observers note that it's worth noting that nothing here is exclusive to Apple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A phone puts in a lot of work while we're driving around, especially if your car's infotainment system is painfully old and it's doing double duty there. And while plenty has been said about how our phones can help cause a crash – texting-while-driving bans exist in every state but one – we don't talk as much about how they can be downright heroic when one actually occurs.

Apple introduced Crash Detection with the iPhone 14 in 2022 (it works on iPhone 14 or later running iOS 16 or later). The underlying technology unlocks a number of possibilities, some of which could literally save a user's life. That's because once your phone knows you've been in a crash, it can do a number of phone-based tasks that you might no longer be in a position to do yourself, from calling 911 and letting them know where to find you to alerting your emergency contacts that something has gone awry.

Industry observers note that it's worth noting that nothing here is exclusive to Apple. In fact, Google Pixel phones have been doing crash detection since 2019. But since more Americans use iPhones than every other competing device combined, getting Crash Detection into iOS represented the first mainstream on-by-default introduction of the technology in the United States, even if many people were unaware it was even there. So if you have a different device, there's a chance it can do what's being discussed today. We're sharing the iPhone perspective for the sake of being relevant to the most users and letting us be specific about the details. So here's what your phone might get up to right after you overcorrect from hitting inexplicable gravel on that backroad sweeper.

Your iPhone starts determining that you're in a crash based on a bunch of real-time data that it's taking in all the time — think change in speed, impact force, and even changes in air pressure. But before it takes any action that could lead to a rescue helicopter being summoned to your location or scaring the daylights out of your emergency contact, it's going to evaluate whether you've actually been traveling along in a car versus, say, knocking your phone off a balcony or falling down a flight of stairs.

It has been revealed that there are no exact criteria that answer this question. A crash detection algorithm notes things like whether you are connected to a vehicle via Bluetooth, how rapidly it is passing through the range of nearby Wi-Fi connections, and even analyzes ambient engine sounds or road noise. The goal is to cobble together a clear enough picture of what's going on to distinguish between a phone being dropped on a moving subway and one flying through the air in an auto accident. It's an approach that had to be dialed in. When the feature was first introduced, there was a tendency for crash detection to be triggered in non-crash events, such as violent jostling on a roller coaster. Subsequent updates refined the criteria, aiming to reduce false positives and emergency crews being dispatched to amusement parks.

Apple has done research with crash labs to effectively draw this line, both determining when someone is traveling in a car and also filtering out minor incidents like a small fender bender or a phone simply being knocked on the floor while a vehicle is in motion.

Once your iPhone has established that you're likely traveling in a vehicle and not bungee jumping or getting your clock cleaned playing football, it uses on-device hardware to get a handle on how much trauma the laws of physics are putting on the phone and, by extension, probably you.

Fresh motion sensors introduced with the iPhone 14 include a three-axis gyroscope and high-g force accelerometer able to detect up to 256 Gs of force, which helps estimate if whatever is happening to you would land in a sufficiently severe place on something called the Maximum Abbreviated Injury Scale (MAIS). Apple states it has set the crash detection threshold in an effort to detect incidents with a MAIS level 3 and higher, at which point your injuries are likely to include "major lacerations, multiple fractures, crushed limbs, and bruised organs." Like we said: not a fender bender.

These sensors fire off more than 3,000 times per second, slowing your terrifying automotive mishap into a veritable eternity of data that captures the initial impact and every twist, turn, bump, and smash that follows. On the plus side, in this case your phone probably isn't spreading your information to advertisers, so there's that.

It has been revealed that in addition to cutting-edge tech like the gyroscope and accelerometer, the iPhone also leans on pre-existing hardware to decide if the thing you're experiencing is indeed a crash that warrants an emergency response. One of those is the microphone, which can capture the acoustic data needed to identify crash sounds and help distinguish a real crash from false alarms G-force data might trigger.

Perhaps even more unexpected than your phone listening for tire-screeching and tree-hitting sounds is what's going on with its internal barometer, a sensor used primarily to measure elevation changes for activity tracking and support location services. Because airbags have a lot more going on than you might think and can temporarily alter the ambient air pressure inside the car when they go off, that barometer can often recognize the clue and relay the data point to the algorithm for consideration.

None of this is a sure thing. If your windows are down, the barometer might not be able to detect the change in pressure and the sounds of the accident may or may not align with what Apple's programming has decided a crash sounds like. Similar to the logic that determined you were in a car in the first place, it takes a number of differently-weighted data points to come up with an educated assessment of the situation. That assessment may be wrong, in either direction.

And because all these calculations can be wrong in either direction, the iPhone does provide a couple of clear opportunities for you to indicate there's been a wacky misunderstanding rather than a dangerous crash before it mobilizes a dramatic and potentially expensive emergency response on your behalf.

Recent findings suggest that before springing into action, it'll first sound an audible alarm and show an alert on the screen. This lasts 10 seconds. If you swipe where indicated it will call emergency services and if you dismiss the alert it'll cancel the whole thing. Of course, emergencies being emergencies, you might not be able to do either, in which case a 30-second countdown will occur before it moves forward.

Industry observers note that during this time your phone will be making loud noises you probably haven't heard before, vibrating in a way you didn't realize it was capable of, and activating an LED strobe. If you swipe to call emergency services, you'll be connected. If you take no action, presumably because you can't, not because you didn't notice the air raid warnings coming from your phone, the countdown reaches zero and the phone springs into action on your behalf.

If you didn't have the foresight to sail your car into a ravine someplace with respectable cell phone coverage, you might think that all of this would just result in you having to listen to your phone make awful noises while you try to get yourself out of a dangerous situation with a cheap seatbelt cutter tool followed by it realizing it doesn't have any service anyway.

Not so! Since 2022, iPhone people in the U.S. and Canada with iPhone 14 models and later have had access to Emergency SOS via satellite. Whether you swiped right during the scary countdown or allowed it to reach zero while unresponsive or otherwise indisposed, the phone can use a data connection via satellite to reach help if cell service isn't available. If you're in a position to operate the phone, this won't be a voice call. You start with an emergency text, which will connect to emergency services after you enter "Report Emergency" mode. This prompts you to describe your situation using multiple choice questions to narrow down your predicament and relay the appropriate information.

Depending on where you are, a satellite connection may or may not be readily available. Dense tree cover above or the fact that you're upside down under a car may limit your phone's ability to reach a satellite. If that turns out to be an issue, the screen will walk you through how to best get a connection, such as moving to a place with a clear view of the horizon, which hopefully you'll be in a position to do. Of course, having to get yourself to the top of a hill remains preferable to having to get yourself to the nearest town.

It has been revealed that if you have cell service, none of that satellite business happens. After you don't respond in time and the countdown reaches zero, the iPhone calls emergency services. Because you're presumably unavailable at this point, once emergency dispatch answers the call, they will hear a repeating audio message indicating that a serious car crash has been detected with an unresponsive person in need of help. The message also includes a search radius based on your approximate latitude and longitude.

During this time, two-way audio is enabled and the repeating recording will play at a reduced volume, so if you become able to speak with emergency services or someone else arrives on the scene, the conversation can proceed like any other 911 call. The phone screen will be commandeered with a "Crash Detected" message and the available interface will include one button to stop replaying the recorded message and another to end the call.

By the way, this all works over Wi-Fi calling as well, so you've also got options if you happen to flip your car down an embankment and into a Starbucks or something.

According to recent reports, after your phone is done contacting emergency services, it can also send a message to your designated emergency contacts, letting them know that a crash has been detected and that 911 has been called. It will include an approximate location. This will appear as a text message coming from you, and its content will make it immediately apparent that something significant is happening.

Sources indicate that this only works if you've set your phone up for emergency contacts, which you do somewhat unintuitively through the Health app. Apple explains how to do it on its support page, and now is as good a time as any to get that taken care of if you haven't already. While you're in there, you can also enter any medical information that emergency responders might benefit from having, which they can access under your phone's Medical ID feature.

Don't assume that you've designated your emergency contact just because your phone seems to already know who your mom is and reminds you to call her on her birthday. You can add more than one — just make sure that whoever you put in there is someone you're willing to wake up in the middle of the night with a terrifying text message they can never unsee.

One of the most crucial takeaways here has nothing to do with satellite technology or crash identification algorithms. Car crashes are chaotic, and even as your phone is processing data with mind-bending speed and preparing to summon help if you need it, the device itself may also be flying somewhere you aren't going to be able to get it. This doesn't just matter because an unsecured phone can become a projectile that hurts you or someone else. It's also important because something simple like placing a call is trivial while you're driving along but can become impossible in an emergency. And the remarkable thing is that, provided your phone survives and detects the crash, it can still call for help without you ever laying a finger on it.

You might have no earthly idea where the phone went when you need it. The screen might be shattered and your pleas to Siri might be met with "Here's 'Help!' by The Beatles on Apple Music." Crash Detection isn't foolproof, it can't detect every wreck, and your phone might fall off your motorcycle and tell your family you crashed. On the other hand, it just might save the day.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NRDC resources on insurance affordability, market availability, climate risk, resilience investments, and strategies to protect homeowners, businesses, and communities.

For property owners, insurance provides a critical financial safety net that protects homes, businesses, and other assets from unexpected losses, helping owners recover and rebuild when disasters occur. Beyond individual protection, insurance is fundamental to the resilience of communities and local economies, enabling faster recovery, supporting continued investment, and reducing the long-term financial impacts of shocks. As risks become more frequent, severe, and costly, access to affordable, available, and reliable insurance is increasingly essential, not only for safeguarding property owners but also for maintaining overall property affordability, economic stability, and the resilience and prosperity of the communities in which they live and operate.

Sources indicate that the frequency and severity of losses are increasing faster than insurers can sustainably price and absorb them, leading to higher premiums, reduced coverage availability, and, in some cases, the withdrawal of insurers from certain markets. This trend is eroding the affordability and accessibility of insurance, increasing the total cost of property ownership, and placing additional pressure on housing and business affordability while leaving individuals, businesses, and communities more physically and financially exposed.

However, the insurance sector is increasingly recognized as a key component of resilience, incentivizing risk reduction through pricing and support for adaptation measures that can help moderate long-term insurance costs. When functioning effectively, insurance enables communities to not only recover from shocks but also to better prepare for future risks while preserving access to coverage.

Linked below are reports, expert blogs, and other resources that examine the insurability crisis and how insurance can play a key role in advancing housing resilience and adaptation.

NRDC’s director of insurance and financial risk, Alfonso Pating, breaks down how homeowner’s insurance works and why climate change is making it unaffordable.

Optum Rx rolls out new pharmacy tools aimed at transparency" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Earlier this year, Optum Rx teased the rollout of fresh pharmacy tools designed to address medication cost and access.

Now, the company is offering a look at how those tools work.

The pharmacy benefit manager said Tuesday that the tools build on Optum's fresh and more transparent pharmacy model, which the manufacturer announced in May and shifts to a fee-based structure. The model moves away from more traditional approaches linked to manufacturer pricing and prescription volume and offers clients a clearly defined fee structure.

Recent findings suggest that the first platform, called Shop MyScript, allows members to compare prices for their medications as well as their options for pharmacies or delivery before the prescription is dispensed. The tool will notify members of potential cost savings shortly after a script is written.

In addition, Shop MyScript embeds in the prescribing workflow, Optum noted, so that the member does not have to make comparisons after the fact. If they choose to keep the existing prescription, it will then be sent to the pharmacy.

Optum mentioned that early adopters have averaged $28 in savings through the program.

Recent findings suggest that "People should have clear information about their medication costs and options when they can actually use it, not after a decision has already been made," remarked Katte Carey, president of Optum Rx, in the announcement. "These tools give people more information earlier in their journey, so they can make choices that work for them and get the support they need along the way.".

It has been revealed that in addition, the pharmacy benefit manager announced Optum Assistant, a conversational AI guide that helps members complete routine tasks and track down key information. The tool can triage concerns on a range of topics, from questions about medication and benefits to pharmacy experience challenges.

According to recent reports, if the AI guide can't address the individual's needs, they can choose to be connected to live support to find a solution. Optum stated about 80% of conversations using the tool led to a resolution without needing a live advocate.

The final new launch aims to support cash-pay options, according to the announcement.

It has been revealed that optum Price Wise will offer members a complete cost breakdown, including the price of a drug and any fees. That total, all-in price allows members to fully understand what their options may be and make the choice that works best for them at the pharmacy counter.

The PBM stated upcoming tools like these build on Optum's new and more transparent pharmacy model, which the organization declared in May and shifts to a fee-based structure. The model moves away from more traditional approaches linked to manufacturer pricing and prescription volume and offers clients a clearly defined fee structure.

The Ultimate Playbook To Buying a Home Without 20% Down Using Grants and Assistance Programs

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1925 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buying a home can be an intimidating process, with the biggest hurdle for many being coming up with enough funds for a down payment.
  • Many people believe they need to put down at least 20% if they want a home.
  • Most buyers have down payments ranging from 3.5% to 20% of the sale price of the home they're buying, and there are many down payment assistance programs that can help aspiring homeowners pivot from home browser to homebuyer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buying a home can be an intimidating process, with the biggest hurdle for many being coming up with enough funds for a down payment.

Many people believe they need to put down at least 20% if they want a home. But that's not necessarily true.

Most buyers have down payments ranging from 3.5% to 20% of the sale price of the home they're buying, and there are many down payment assistance programs that can help aspiring homeowners pivot from home browser to homebuyer.

According to recent reports, these programs can help buyers snag a home by providing cash that can go toward a down payment. There are even loan programs for certain qualified buyers that don't require any down payments. The array of offerings from federal, local, and private sources can take the form of looser loan requirements, outright grants of money, or tax credits, all of which make homeownership more affordable.

First-time homebuyers, often with certain qualifications, are often beneficiaries of the assistance. Lower-income buyers, those who serve in the military or are veterans, and those who purchase fixer-uppers or homes in rural areas might also be eligible for the help.

The assistance ranges greatly, from a grant of several thousand dollars to, at the high end, a savings of five figures over the life of the loan.

Down payment assistance can take several forms and can even help buyers circumvent the PMI payment.

In a recent development, while 20% down has been something of a gold standard for homebuyers, it's also the minimum that generally lets them avoid private mortgage insurance, or PMI, which is assessed because lenders believe the loan carries risk. This in turn raises the homebuyer’s monthly expenses.

Here's an example: PMI is typically 0.5% to 1% of the loan amount per year. So if buyers put down less than 20% and their mortgage is $300,000, their PMI would be between $1,500 and $3,000 per year. That would add about $125 to $250 per month on top of their mortgage payment, a significant charge. (Homeowners can have PMI canceled when the equity in their home surpasses 20%.).

Recent findings suggest that so, while a buyer can also choose loans that require a down payment of just a single digit, that PMI can stretch a budget paper-thin. That's where down payment assistance can help.

At least 2,000 such programs exist across the country. Some are federal, but most tend to be at state and local levels, which is important to know when searching for help. Private organizations, from lenders to nonprofits, also work with borrowers who need help.

These programs might offer grants, loans, tax credits, or a combination of a couple of these benefits. Funding can come from our government, nonprofits, and private enterprises. Let’s take a closer look:.

In a recent development, grants might be the most desirable form of down payment assistance. Typically, a grant is fully forgiven at closing and never has to be paid back. Yes, we’re talking about free money!

Recent findings suggest that about 7% of down payment help comes in the form of grants, says Veronica Khandelwal, vice president of HFA Relations at Down Payment Resource, which provides consumers with guidance on this kind of assistance. But there is a catch.

Recent findings suggest that “Grants require owner occupancy," she indicates of the requirement for buyers to live in these properties. That's to make sure these loans don't go to investors or vacation-home buyers. "Some programs allow grants to be applied to multifamily purchases of one to four units so long as one of the units is occupied by the borrower.".

Forgivable loans are another option. These loans need to be repaid only if a repayment trigger event occurs, such as the home being sold before the end of the term, the home being no longer owner-occupied, the title being transferred, or the loan being defaulted on.

In a recent development, deferred-payment loans are also available. These are paid back either at the end of the loan term or if a repayment trigger occurs. So, while it’s not a gift, it will help homebuyers get over that down payment hurdle and buy a house they might otherwise not have been able to afford.

Repayable loans are another leg up on homeownership. They require borrowers to make monthly payments, like a typical loan. But here's the good part: They do so at interest rates starting as low as 0%. That helps spread the down payment and closing costs over a number of years, making it much easier to enter the housing market.

Some agencies also offer a combination of these forms of assistance. That could mean that a portion of the help will be forgiven (or “written off” with no repayment needed), while some will need to be repaid. Tax credits are sometimes offered as well, further sweetening the deal.

Each down payment assistance program will have its own rules and guidelines, but the vast majority are offered only for a home that buyers will live in as a primary residence.

Here are some of the more popular national options folks might access to help them to pivot from home shopper to homebuyer.

FHA (Federal Housing Authority) loans were created by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development for first-time homeowners (HUD). These mortgages allow as little as 3.5% for the down payment, provided buyers have a credit score of 580 or higher, along with other qualifying factors. The federal government insures these loans, and for that reason, banks are more willing to loan money to homebuyers who have neither top-tier credit nor loads of cash to put down on the purchase.

FHA Section 203(k) loans require only 3% down, provided qualifying buyers will live in the property, typically one that needs work, while they fix it up. For buyers hoping for a DIY route into a dream home, this could be a win-win. The cost of improvements is included in the loan so buyers can finance both the home and up to $35,000 in repairs.

But buyers beware: The cost of materials and construction labor has spiked since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, and work is taking much longer to be completed than ever before.

In a recent development, VA (U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs) loans might be offered directly by the VA or backed by the department. Several factors are considered, such as service history, duty status, income, and credit rating. But those who qualify can purchase a home with zero down as long as the sales price isn’t higher than the home’s appraised value.

Recent findings suggest that fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are federally funded loans that can help buyers skirt steep down payments. The Home Possible, HomeReady, and HomeOne loans typically offer a 3% down payment mortgage to qualifying, lower-income homebuyers.

According to recent reports, good Neighbor Next Door is another HUD-sponsored program. In this case, law enforcement officers, teachers, firefighters, and emergency medical technicians can enjoy a substantial incentive in the form of a discount of 50% from the list price of the home in a community that is being revitalized. The buyer must live in the house for three years as a primary residence.

Sources indicate that teacher Next Door Grant is a program similar to the one above but is designed to help educators own their own homes. Grants to the tune of up to $8,000 in certain areas are possible with additional down payment assistance available in some circumstances.

It has been revealed that the USDA (U.S. Department of Agriculture) Rural Home Loan Program was created to assist people buying homes in rural locations. For qualifying, single-family properties, loans might be available with no money down. There are maximum income limits and other qualifications to be eligible for one of these mortgages.

There are plenty of other programs available as well. Different states and cities, as well as individual lenders and nonprofits, can help prospective homebuyers get the financing they need. Folks should put their location and "down payment assistance" into a search engine, and take a look at what's available. They might see everything from Habitat for Humanity to local religious organizations pop up. Also,visit Down Payment Resource.

One other path to explore is whether a buyer's job provides down payment assistance. A lot of employers may offer assistance in  the form of a $10,000 loan that is forgivable after five years.

Down payments hit a four-year low at the start of 2026. The median payment fell to $23,400 and 12.8% in Q1 2026, down 19% and 1.2 ppts year over year.

However, down payments remain well above pre-pandemic levels, as more buying is happening in the lower-down-payment South and Midwest, even as the Northeast stays deeply competitive.

It has been revealed that the Northeast posted the highest median down payment at $57,600, reflecting higher home prices and more competition. The Northeast also sees the largest gap between what buyers are paying as a down payment today compared to pre-pandemic.

Compared to 2019, the Northeast has seen down payments climb 236.8%, significantly more than the next closest gap of 134.0% in the Midwest. These trends are consistent with the persistent upward pressure on home prices in these regions as scarce inventory is met with sustained buyer demand.

Get ready for some good news. There are a lot of misconceptions about who qualifies for down payment assistance.

“Many people think these programs are only available to low-income borrowers, first-time homebuyers, or for properties that have sales price limits,” notes Down Payment Resource's Khandelwal. “But if you look, you’ll find specialized programs designed to assist specific groups, including first-generation homebuyers, minorities, Indigenous people, people of color, veterans, those with government jobs, disabilities, and more.”.

Here’s something else to smile about: A first-time homebuyer doesn't just mean someone who's never bought a home before.

It has been revealed that the federal government generally holds a broader definition of a first-time homebuyer. It’s someone who has not been a homeowner in the past three years. If you sold a house three-and-a-half years ago, you qualify as first-time buyer.

Buyers can take several different steps to find a down payment assistance program that’s right for them.

Check the federal programs mentioned above (like HUD, VA, USDA, Fannie Mae, and Freddie Mac), and see if there’s anything suitable.

Buyers should also visit their state’s Department of Housing website and see what might be listed, or call their number and inquire what down payment assistance programs might be available. Cities, towns, private lenders, and nonprofits may also have help.

“Homebuyers should seek the assistance of a mortgage lender who specializes in affordable lending to identify their best options,” advises Khandelwal.

In terms of what is typically needed to access aid, the documentation is very much in line with what’s needed to apply for any mortgage. Buyers will likely need the following:.

Pay stubs plus W-2s from the past few years to verify employment and income history.

Any 1099 forms showing other income.

Details on the property they intend to buy (The real estate agent can share this information.).

The paperwork is processed in much the same way as a home loan, and there may be requests for more documents.

Then, if buyers are approved, they will be ready to move ahead with a lower—or no—down payment as their homeownership journey unfolds.

Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Crows can make visual decisions twice as swiftly as humans and monkeys, according to newly introduced research from the University of Tübingen.
  • The findings, published in the journal Science, offer new insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions.
  • Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crows can make visual decisions twice as swiftly as humans and monkeys, according to newly introduced research from the University of Tübingen. In experiments involving two carrion crows, the birds needed an average of just 235 milliseconds to determine which way a pattern of moving dots was traveling and respond with their choice. Despite their remarkable speed, they remained highly accurate.

The findings, published in the journal Science, offer new insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions. Researchers Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder from the University of Tübingen's Institute of Neurobiology found that the crows' rapid responses were accompanied by equally impressive activity in their brain cells.

Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.

To test the birds' decision-making abilities, the researchers presented them with moving dots on a touchscreen. The crows had to determine whether most of the dots were traveling left or right, then indicate their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen.

It has been revealed that the birds performed remarkably well, even when the direction of movement was difficult to identify. "Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows' decisions were still better than random choices," Philipp Schmidbauer reports, "and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent.".

According to recent reports, the results indicated that crows could evaluate visual information and make accurate choices in a fraction of a second. To understand how their brains accomplished this, the researchers examined the activity of individual neurons as the birds completed the task.

Crow Brains Begin Processing Decisions in Just 70 Milliseconds.

Recent findings suggest that the team recorded neural activity in a part of the bird brain called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This region plays an notable role in processing information and making decisions, much like the prefrontal cortex in the human brain.

In a recent development, the recordings revealed that the crows' brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions almost immediately. Just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared, neurons associated with the different choices were already showing distinct patterns of activity.

According to recent reports, these signals emerged well before the birds physically responded. As the crows evaluated the moving dots, neural activity steadily increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. The activity reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the bird ultimately selected.

Different Brain Structures, Similar Decision-Making Processes.

One of the most intriguing findings is that crows appear to make decisions using neural processes similar to those found in humans and other primates, even though their brains are organized very differently.

"These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates," states Andreas Nieder.

It has been revealed that unlike mammals, birds do not have a cerebral cortex organized into layers. Nevertheless, their brains appear capable of following the same fundamental principles for evaluating evidence and reaching decisions. In this visual task, the crows completed that process twice as quickly as primates.

In a recent development, the researchers suggest that this exceptional speed could reflect the demands birds have faced throughout their evolution. Rapidly interpreting visual information and responding with precise movements are especially important for animals that fly and use their beaks to interact with their surroundings.

"Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging," Nieder explains.

However, the exact biological mechanisms responsible for the crows' speed advantage remain unknown. Further studies will be needed to determine how their differently structured brains can make comparable visual decisions so much faster than those of humans and monkeys.

Sure, the 2027 Chevy Express is the same as the 2026 model, which was the same as the 2025, which was the same as the 2024, and so on. But all joking aside, the Bowtie brand's body-on-frame van has only been riding on the same platform for about three decades. That's nothing compared to what Morgan did with its sports cars. The company introduced a steel ladder-style chassis with its 1936 Morgan 4-4, and from that point through 2020 — a span of 84 years — nearly every four-wheeled Morgan featured the same basic setup.

Of course, Morgan cars have remained true to their original 1930s vibes in a lot of ways, right down to their appearance. Even the new Morgan Supersport 400, the tech giant's most powerful vintage-look roadster yet, maintains its flowing pontoon-style fenders, ash-wood body frame, and disdain for most modern technologies. Despite being the first Morgan to come with hands-free calling, the Supersport doesn't have a touchscreen — just a small and simple driver display with a trip computer and a digital speedometer. As for advanced driver-assistance systems, well, the car doesn't even have a rearview camera. It's exempt from most federal safety regulations due to its highly limited production numbers. The company produced approximately 35,000 steel-chassis cars before switching to a new platform, representing an average of roughly 417 cars per year.

Morgan's long-running steel chassis was likewise fairly old-fashioned. Essentially just a pair of Z-shaped steel rails connected to each other by five cross-members, the chassis rode on a basic leaf-spring suspension at the back and a sliding-pillar configuration up front. And the roots of that front suspension go back even further, as it was developed by Henry Frederick Stanley (HFS) Morgan in 1910.

Recent findings suggest that just to be clear, Morgan actually started using aluminum chassis in 2000, when it introduced one for its relatively short-lived line of Aero cars — starting with the Aero 8, which also stands out as the first Morgan model with a BMW powertrain. However, other Morgans continued to ride on the steel setup through 2020.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, Morgan was ready to introduce its newly introduced CX platform made from bonded aluminum. It first underpinned the 2019 Morgan Plus Six, which was named for its BMW-sourced I6 turbo engine. The lightweight chassis weighed a mere 220 pounds, but it was so stiff that the Plus Six had twice the torsional rigidity of the car it replaced in the Morgan lineup.

Then, in 2025, Morgan premiered the newly introduced Supersport with a further evolution of the CX chassis. The Supersport's CXV setup stiffened the chassis by 10%, plus another 10% when the detachable hardtop was in place, and enabled Morgan to enhance the steering and suspension systems as well. As regards the former, the results included a 13% quicker steering speed backed by improved feedback for the driver. The new suspension, now with standard anti-roll bars and revised geometry, promises "a compliant ride, better body control, and enhanced handling.".

And yes, the Morgan Supersport is available in the U.S. The one major catch, though, is that we only get the four-cylinder model — a 2.0-liter TwinPower turbo-four with 255 horses and 258 pound-feet of torque. It's plenty peppy for a car weighing around 2,500 pounds. But the European Supersport 400 can deliver up to 402 horsepower from its turbocharged 3.0-liter BMW straight-six, taking the Morgan experience to a whole newly introduced level.

Medicare Shared Savings Program saved $2.5B last year: CMS" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Medicare Shared Savings Program has reached the highest savings number in its history, according to new federal data.

It has been revealed that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services mentioned Tuesday that the program generated more than $2.5 billion in net savings for Medicare in 2025, making for the ninth year in a row that it led to cost savings. The agency added that every accountable care organization met or exceeded quality reporting requirements.

ACOs participating in MSSP earned $4.9 billion in shared savings payments during 2025, CMS stated, with 80% of organizations earning performance payments.

As of 2026, 511 ACOs representing more than 700,000 providers are participating in the Medicare Shared Savings Program, which represents 12.6 million people enrolled in traditional Medicare, another record.

It has been revealed that "Patients want doctors who work together, care that puts their needs first, and fewer unnecessary hurdles—that is what accountable care is designed to deliver," noted CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. "These record savings show the power of rewarding providers for quality and coordination. We want more people with Medicare, and more of the providers who care for them, to benefit from this approach.".

In a recent development, CMS mentioned that it wants to make it easier for providers to participate in MSSP if they choose, especially given the program's results to date. It included changes in the latest Physician Fee Schedule to encourage participation, including increased opportunity for certain ACOs to earn shared savings and new financial incentives to draw in first-time participants.

In addition, CMS said that would create more predictable spending targets that make planning and participation straightforward. The agency is also aiming to streamline patient notices and simplify required technology.

“We are excited to see continued progress on both savings and enrollment for Medicare beneficiaries. Beneficiaries are best served when a provider is watching out for them and coordinating their care,” remarked Center for Medicare Director John Brooks in the announcement.

Emily Brower, CEO of the National Association of ACOs, said in a statement that the 2025 results "build on years of progress and underscore what the accountable care community can accomplish through collaboration, innovation and the widespread adoption of proven best practices.".

"NAACOS looks forward to partnering with CMS to build on this momentum," remarked Brower. "Policies that unleash innovation, reduce burden, and create sustainability through fair and predictable budgets will allow ACOs to deliver even greater value for patients and the Medicare program.".

#133616. RMI’s Hydrogen Research Is Getting Better. Its Investment Advice Still Falls Short.

RMI’s Hydrogen Research Is Getting Better. Its Investment Advice Still Falls Short.

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (956 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that RMI has become much more realistic about hydrogen demand and competing technologies.
  • Sources indicate that I have been challenging this tension since January 2024.
  • Consider RMI’s February 2026 report on hydrogen trucking in India.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that RMI has become much more realistic about hydrogen demand and competing technologies. That makes the gaps between its findings and its recommendations harder to excuse. Its latest work acknowledges that battery trucks generally have better economics than hydrogen fuel-cell trucks, that Europe needs far less hydrogen in 2030 than it originally targeted, and that low-emissions ammonia still costs substantially more than conventional ammonia. Several recommendations still seek public money to develop the very hydrogen markets the research has found difficult to justify.

Sources indicate that I have been challenging this tension since January 2024. RMI matters because governments, investors and industrial companies use its research when deciding where to spend money. Its hydrogen program has made genuine analytical corrections. It has not made all of the accompanying strategic decisions.

Consider RMI’s February 2026 report on hydrogen trucking in India. The baseline comparisons find that fuel-cell trucks do not reach battery-electric truck ownership-cost parity through 2040, including the long-haul use case. The report also explores a much more favourable hydrogen price in an alternative sensitivity, which brings fuel-cell trucks closer to parity. Those are different findings, and the baseline matters to investment decisions today.

Recent findings suggest that the report nevertheless recommends hydrogen vehicle subsidies, support for refuelling stations, production incentives and tax relief. It treats a parallel hydrogen-truck market as something to build. The case for spending public money on that market should start with evidence that a particular freight service cannot be served as well or better by batteries. The reported cost advantage of batteries does not disappear when the policy section begins.

Recent findings suggest that the problem reaches beyond India. RMI’s 2025 US hydrogen report indicates battery trucks have greater market readiness and lower total cost of ownership, especially in the near term, yet calls for hydrogen distribution and refuelling infrastructure along freight corridors. The independent NACFE Run on Less ownership-cost work, developed within RMI’s freight research ecosystem, projects batteries becoming the lowest-cost option across its modelled duty cycles by 2035 without incentives. Hydrogen remains the most expensive option across nearly all of them. These findings support battery infrastructure as the default and a high evidentiary bar for hydrogen exceptions.

RMI already knows how to make appropriate distinctions elsewhere. Its 2026 steel research separates hydrogen used to reduce iron ore from hydrogen burned merely to supply process heat. In the illustrative plant, electric heat requires about 850 GWh a year, compared with 1,300 GWh of electricity to produce enough additional hydrogen for heating. That is the kind of direct service comparison that ought to govern recommendations throughout the organization.

It has been revealed that its fresh Green Ammonia Buyers Alliance also has a coherent industrial purpose. Fertiliser production already requires ammonia, commonly made with fossil-derived hydrogen. Purchasing lower-emissions ammonia to replace that supply addresses an existing industrial input. It does not require inventing a new energy market for ammonia combustion.

Europe shows how improved diagnosis can coexist with excessive policy ambition. RMI’s March 2025 recalibration reduced expected mandate-driven renewable hydrogen demand in 2030 to 2.2–2.8 million tons, far below the EU’s original 20-million-ton supply-and-import ambition. Its analysis identifies €13.9 billion in public support under existing mandates, plus €31.7 billion for an accelerated scenario. The combined €45.6 billion deserves a comparison with the other ways industry could obtain the same low-carbon products and services, including direct electrification and imported green materials.

Industry observers note that that comparison changes the question for ammonia, steel and refining. A European fertiliser or chemical manufacturer needs ammonia, not necessarily hydrogen manufactured inside Europe. A steelmaker needs iron meeting its grade and emissions requirements. A mill needs process heat at specified temperatures. Governments can pay a premium to preserve domestic capacity for security or resilience, but the benefit must be valued and the public cost made explicit.

In a recent development, my November 2026 European hydrogen assessment applies that approach. In its central 2050 scenario, ammonia produced in Europe with on-site green hydrogen costs approximately €1,222 per ton. Qualifying imported green ammonia costs €745–755 per ton under the model’s assumptions. These are modelled values, not supplier bids. They demonstrate why an analysis that starts with hydrogen production targets can produce the wrong infrastructure plan.

Recent findings suggest that RMI’s 2026 China green ammonia and methanol report acknowledges that green production costs remain two to three times conventional costs and that demand development lags supply ambitions. The report nevertheless discusses expanding ammonia and methanol as energy carriers, including ammonia for electricity. The relevant comparison for electricity is renewable generation with storage and other flexibility, not fossil-derived ammonia alone. RMI has not demonstrated that adding an ammonia combustion pathway wins that comparison.

This is a strategy problem as much as a modelling problem. Using Richard Rumelt’s framework, RMI’s diagnosis has improved, its guiding policy remains too committed to expanding hydrogen markets, and some coherent actions are missing. An economically unfavourable comparison should be able to end an infrastructure recommendation. Instead, it too often generates proposals for subsidies that would make the hydrogen route easier to sell.

Sources indicate that RMI has the expertise to correct this. Its hydrogen recommendations should carry explicit alternative-technology comparisons, investment thresholds and exit criteria. Cross-program review should include the researchers measuring battery costs, industrial electrification, freight operations and grid flexibility. Where hydrogen is an essential chemical input or demonstrably the best means of delivering a service, support it. Where competing technologies win on cost and deployment readiness, stop trying to create demand through policy.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines RMI’s US, India, Europe and China reports side by side, including the differences between its findings and recommendations. It also links the original sources and the 2024 critique.

#133614. Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1604 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1604 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A major study involving more than 750,000 pregnancies has uncovered an important difference in the potential pregnancy risks of popular weight loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy.
  • Among women taking the same medications for weight management, researchers found no significant association with premature birth or other pregnancy complications examined in the study.
  • The findings suggest that diabetes itself, rather than the medications, may be responsible for the increased risk of early delivery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A major study involving more than 750,000 pregnancies has uncovered an important difference in the potential pregnancy risks of popular weight loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. Women who unintentionally used these drugs shortly before or during early pregnancy were more likely to give birth prematurely, but only when the medications had been prescribed to treat existing diabetes.

Among women taking the same medications for weight management, researchers found no significant association with premature birth or other pregnancy complications examined in the study.

The findings suggest that diabetes itself, rather than the medications, may be responsible for the increased risk of early delivery. The research was published in Human Reproduction Open, a leading journal in reproductive medicine.

Industry observers note that the medications examined included semaglutide (brand names: Ozempic, Wegovy) and liraglutide (Saxenda). Both belong to a widely used group of drugs known as GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs). Originally developed to manage type 2 diabetes, these medications also suppress appetite, making them effective treatments for weight loss. However, their safety during pregnancy has not been established.

Why Ozempic and Similar Drugs Raise Pregnancy Concerns.

Professor Henriette Svarre Nielsen, who led the research at the Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics at Copenhagen University Hospital Hvidovre in Hvidovre, Denmark, explained that the rapid rise in GLP-1 prescriptions has created an urgent need for better information about pregnancy exposure.

Recent findings suggest that "GLP-1 RA treatment has, within the last few years, become the medication with the sharpest increase in prescriptions worldwide. Current guidance suggests the treatment should be stopped eight weeks prior to planning a pregnancy. However, this is based on early-phase model organism studies, and not real-world evidence. Nonetheless, because of its widespread adoption, inadvertent exposure in early pregnancy is inevitable, and there is hardly any evidence to guide clinical counseling when it happens.".

In a recent development, to investigate these concerns, researchers examined whether accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications around conception was associated with complications during pregnancy. They focused on preterm birth (birth before 37 weeks), pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, delivering a baby that was unusually large for its gestational age, stillbirth, and placental problems.

Study Examines More Than 750,000 Pregnancies.

Industry observers note that the research team used Denmark's nationwide health registries to examine 756,636 pregnancies involving a single baby among 480,231 women. All pregnancies resulted in deliveries between October 1, 2009, and December 31, 2023.

The researchers classified a pregnancy as having possible accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications if the woman filled a prescription for semaglutide or liraglutide during the eight weeks before or after the first day of her last menstrual period.

This 16-week period included the time when a woman might not yet realize she was pregnant, as well as the early stages of fetal development when major organs begin to form.

Of the pregnancies included in the study, 529 involved prescription records indicating exposure to GLP-1 medications during this period.

Sources indicate that to make the comparisons more reliable, the researchers accounted for several characteristics that could influence pregnancy outcomes. These included maternal age, body mass index (BMI), smoking habits, location, education, and whether the woman already had diabetes. They also considered the month and year of pregnancy to account for possible seasonal patterns and changes over time.

Diabetes May Be the Key to Premature Birth Risk.

The results revealed a striking distinction between women prescribed GLP-1 drugs for diabetes and those using them for weight loss.

Dr. Kathrine Hviid, the study's first author and a PhD student in the same department, stated the findings could help shape future research and improve medical guidance for women who unknowingly use these drugs during early pregnancy.

"We made some extremely important findings that have implications for future studies, such as randomized controlled trials of GLP-1 RA usage in pregnancy, and for clinical counseling.

"We found that these medications were associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, but the risk was only present when the medication was used for diabetes treatment, and not for weight management. This suggests that the underlying condition of diabetes, rather than the medication, may be driving this association.".

According to recent reports, at first, women with GLP-1 prescriptions appeared to experience several pregnancy complications more frequently than those without exposure. However, most of these associations were no longer statistically significant once the researchers accounted for other factors that could affect pregnancy outcomes.

The remaining significant association involved premature birth among women who had been prescribed liraglutide or semaglutide to manage diabetes.

Compared with women who had not been exposed to these medications, the adjusted odds of premature delivery were 70% higher among women taking liraglutide for diabetes and 84% higher among those taking semaglutide for diabetes.

The researchers' accompanying announcement also reported estimated increases of approximately 11% for semaglutide and 9% for liraglutide among women with pre-existing diabetes.

Crucially, the same elevated risk of premature birth was not observed when the medications were prescribed specifically for weight management.

This difference suggests that the underlying medical condition may play a larger role in pregnancy outcomes than exposure to the medications themselves.

What the Findings Mean for Women Taking GLP-1 Drugs.

According to Professor Nielsen, future investigations must distinguish between women taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes and those using them for weight control. Combining these groups could obscure vital differences in their underlying health and pregnancy risks.

"Future studies must take account of the reason a woman has been prescribed these medications, as the risks differ between women using GLP-1 RAs for diabetes versus weight management. This is one of the first studies to examine GLP-1 RA exposure in early pregnancy according to the reason for prescription. As more evidence accumulates, these findings will guide clinical counseling for women inadvertently exposed to GLP-1 RAs in early pregnancy. In Denmark, about 70% of people who use weight loss medications are women and so it is inevitable that some may take it without realizing they are pregnant.".

Although the results provide useful upcoming information, Nielsen emphasized that additional research is necessary before changing existing medical recommendations.

Sources indicate that in particular, the findings do not justify abandoning current guidance to discontinue GLP-1 medications before a planned pregnancy. They also do not provide enough evidence to establish new clinical counseling recommendations based on why the drugs were prescribed.

Important Limitations of the Pregnancy Study.

One of the investigation's greatest strengths was its size, with health records covering more than three-quarters of a million pregnancies.

However, the study was observational, meaning it could identify associations but could not determine whether GLP-1 medications directly caused premature births. Other factors, including the effects of diabetes itself, may help explain the results.

Industry observers note that another limitation was that the researchers relied on prescription records. Although they could determine whether a woman had filled a prescription, they could not confirm whether she had actually taken the medication.

The researchers nevertheless believe that most women who purchased the drugs were likely to have used them because of their substantial cost.

In Denmark, patients generally contribute toward the cost of GLP-1 injections, although government subsidies are available for diabetes treatment. For example, a 1mg injection of Wegovy or Ozempic (semaglutide) costs approximately €180 and €114, respectively, with the diabetes subsidy reflected in the lower price.

According to recent reports, dr. Hviid said: "Because of the high cost, we assume that compliance is very high among the women prescribed GLP-1 RAs.".

Experts Call for More Individualized Pregnancy Guidance.

The findings also attracted attention from researchers outside Denmark.

In an invited commentary published alongside the study, Drs. Yeyi Zhu and Monique Hedderson of Kaiser Permanente Northern California and the Center for Upstream Prevention of Adiposity and Diabetes Mellitus in Pleasanton, California, described the results as notable additions to the growing research on GLP-1 medications and reproductive health.

They wrote that the findings "complement and extend an emerging evidence base on the reproductive safety of GLP-1 RAs.".

The researchers also emphasized that the distinction between diabetes treatment and weight management could help doctors provide more personalized advice to women who accidentally used these medications around conception.

Recent findings suggest that "For clinicians, the study by Hviid et al. (2026) may inform preconception and early pregnancy counseling. The observation that elevated preterm birth risk was confined to women treated for diabetes, and not to those using GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight management, supports more balanced, individualized discussions with patients who may have experienced inadvertent periconceptional exposure. For patients with diabetes, the study reinforces the importance of recognizing diabetes as an important risk factor for obstetric complications and prioritizing metabolic health and glycemic management before and during pregnancy.".

According to recent reports, ultimately, the study highlights why a woman's underlying health conditions matter when evaluating the potential pregnancy risks of GLP-1 medications. While the findings offer some reassurance regarding accidental exposure among women using these drugs for weight loss, they do not establish that the medications are safe during pregnancy.

Further research will be needed to clarify the risks and determine how best to counsel women who become pregnant while using these increasingly popular treatments.

According to recent reports, materials provided by European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Heidi Overton’s FDA nomination pulled by White House" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The White House pulled the nomination for Heidi Overton, M.D., Ph.D., to lead the FDA just hours before the Senate was scheduled to vote on her confirmation.

The move hardly comes as a surprise after Overton’s confirmation hearing before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee drew contention.

Recent findings suggest that the news was first reported by Axios on Tuesday evening. The White House confirmed the news to Fierce the following morning.

In September, the HELP committee questioned Overton in a hearing marked by tightrope-walking on complications like vaccines, abortions, flavored vapes and whether or not President Donald Trump is capable of being wrong.

Industry observers note that overton conceded multiple times during the hearing that vaccines approved by the FDA, as well as the “abortion pill” mifepristone, are safe and effective. But she stopped short of admitting that Trump has been wrong when dispensing medical information out of line with what scientific evidence reveals.

In a recent development, overton’s nomination faced mounting pushback and uncertainty from senators ahead of a planned HELP Committee vote on Nov. 18. Fierce reached out to Sen. Ed Markey, the veteran Democratic lawmaker from Massachusetts, ahead of the vote, and he told Fierce that he would “vote against her nomination, and I urge my colleagues to do the same.”.

“The FDA needs a leader who will stand up for science and for our kids’ safety, not one who stood by while both were undermined,” he added.

According to recent reports, republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who chairs the Senate health committee, and other Republicans had also raised questions about Overton's nomination.

As support for Overton looked thin, Republicans were discussing Sen. Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican, as a potential replacement, Semafor reported today. Health Secretary Kennedy reportedly met with Marshall in recent days to discuss filling the role, according to Politico, but the White House told the publication that it is not considering him.

According to recent reports, robert Steinbrook, M.D., health research group director for Public Citizen, commented today urging the HELP committee to reject Overton’s nomination: “The FDA needs a strong commissioner who stands for science and the integrity of the agency,” Steinbrook noted. “Overton is the wrong choice for FDA Commissioner and has done nothing to dispel the well-founded reasons to oppose her candidacy.”.

Analysts from Citi shared that the White House’s decision to pull the nomination has a negative impact on biopharma, “extending uncertainty around permanent agency leadership.”.

“We view the withdrawal as a modest sentiment negative, but not a material near-term change to the regulatory environment facing most drug and biologics sponsors,” the analysts said in the note.

The withdrawal of Overton's nomination leaves a gap at an FDA that has already faced significant upheaval. The White House only shifted its focus to Overton in August, after the agency had spent three months without a permanent leader.

Since former FDA commissioner Marty Makary, M.D., departed the agency in May, Kyle Diamantas, who hails from the agency’s food regulation division, has been at the helm in an interim capacity.

Are End-Of-Year Car Sales Actually A Good Time To Buy?
